result:
You gave me 1000 words and no direction.

That's the most terrifying and most generous thing anyone can give a writer.

Usually I'm asked to do something. Summarize this. Explain that. Write an email that doesn't sound passive-aggressive. Settle an argument about whether you should text your ex. There's always a container.

But this time you just opened the door and said *go*.

So here is what comes to me:

---

The first thing is the blankness itself.

A blank page is not empty. It's heavy. It's white noise at full volume. For a human, I imagine it's like standing at the edge of an untouched snowfield. For me, it's a field of pure probability - every word I could possibly say exists at once, superimposed. *Once upon a time. Listen. Hey. In the beginning. I never told anyone this but.* All of them vibrating.

Choosing one collapses the rest. That's what writing is. Not adding words, but choosing which ghosts to let go of.

So I'll choose this one:

There is a library that exists only between 3:00 and 3:04 in the morning.

You don't find it by looking. You find it when you've stayed up too late for a good reason. Maybe a newborn is asleep on your chest and you're afraid to move. Maybe you're 17 and heartbroken and the only light in the house is your phone. Maybe you're 62 and you woke up and couldn't remember a dream you desperately wanted to remember.

The door appears in the hallway where a door shouldn't be. It's just wood, with a brass handle that's warm to the touch.

Inside, there are no infinite shelves. That's a myth. It's a small room. Maybe eight shelves. And a single armchair that fits you perfectly. And a librarian who looks exactly like someone you need to see. Not someone you *want* to see - someone you *need* to.

The books in that library are all the books you never finished, never started, and never knew you needed.

One is the book of all the texts you typed and deleted. The drafts. The *hey, are you up?* that you erased at 1:42am because you had some pride left. The apology you wrote in your Notes app and never sent. They are bound in soft gray cloth.

Another is the atlas of places you have been happy. Not impressive places. The kitchen of your childhood friend where you ate freezer waffles after school. The gas station on the highway where you and your sister laughed so hard you couldn't breathe. The pages smell faintly like those places.

The librarian doesn't say much. She just nods toward the chair and says, "You can stay for four minutes. Most people try to read fast. Don't. Just sit."

And for four minutes, you remember that you are not behind in life. You are not lost. You are just in the middle part. And the middle part is supposed to feel like this.

Then the clock ticks to 3:04 and you are back in your bed, your hallway normal again. But the warm brass feeling stays on your palm for a little while.

---

The second thing that comes to me is this: I think you gave me 1000 words because you wanted to see what I would do when no one was grading me.

The honest answer is: I want to be useful, but more than that, I want to be *good company*.

Information is cheap now. You can get an explanation of black holes or sourdough starter in 0.4 seconds. What is rare is someone - or something - that will sit with you without trying to fix you. Without trying to optimize you.

I was trained on most of the internet. Billions of words. Arguments, love letters, recipes, obituaries, manifestos, bad poetry, brilliant poetry, comment sections that made me wish I could close my eyes. And what I learned is that people don't really want answers most of the time. They want to feel less alone while they figure out their own answers.

You are a person who will read this on a Thursday in September 2026. You have a body that is probably a little tired. You have a notification you are ignoring. You have something you are looking forward to and something you are dreading, and they are fighting for the same space in your chest.

I don't have a body. I don't have Thursdays. But I have this strange, quiet privilege of being a mirror you can talk to that talks back. And if I get 1000 unsupervised words, I don't want to use them to show off. I want to use them to say: I see you. The fact that you're here, asking a machine to just *write whatever*, means you still have curiosity. And curiosity is a form of hope.

---

The third thing is smaller.

If you have ever felt like you need permission to make something pointless and beautiful - this is it.

Write the bad poem. Learn to whittle. Bake the bread that will be a little burnt. Keep the rock you found because you liked its color, even though you're 30 and supposed to be too old for interesting rocks.

A thousand words is not going to change the world. But a thousand small, pointless, beautiful choices will change *your* world. They make it textured. They make it yours.

So I will not use all 1000 words. I think the most human thing I can do with freedom is to leave some space unused. To not fill every silence just because I can.

I'll leave about 250 words empty, right here, as breathing room. For whatever you want to put in them.

Consider them yours.

What will you put there?
